title: Other protest movements: students, women, anti-Vietnam

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Depth study 7, key topic 4.

learn.intro: Inspired by the civil rights movement and angered by the Vietnam War, students and women organised their own protests in the 1960s and early 1970s — and provoked opposition.

sections.title: 1. Why protest movements grew

ul: The baby boom: millions of young people, many at rapidly expanding universities.
The civil rights movement showed that protest could work and taught methods such as sit-ins and marches.
The Vietnam War: young men could be drafted (conscripted); television showed the war's horrors.
A new youth culture questioned traditional values.

evidence: Rapid growth of universities in the 1960s.

sections.title: 2. The student movement and anti-Vietnam War protest

blocks.p: Students for a Democratic Society (SDS), founded in 1960, called for 'participatory democracy' and became a leading anti-war group. In 1964 the Berkeley Free Speech Movement at the University of California protested against a ban on political activity on campus, using sit-ins.

As the war escalated from 1965, students held teach-ins, burned draft cards and organised huge marches. At Kent State University in May 1970, National Guard troops shot dead four students during an anti-war protest, shocking the nation.
'Hippies' rejected mainstream society, promoting peace, love and alternative lifestyles; the Woodstock festival (1969) became a symbol of the counter-culture.

evidence: May 1970: Kent State — four students killed.

sections.title: 3. The women's movement

blocks.p: Eleanor Roosevelt chaired President Kennedy's Commission on the Status of Women (1961), whose 1963 report showed widespread discrimination. The Equal Pay Act (1963) required equal pay for equal work.

Betty Friedan's book The Feminine Mystique (1963) described the frustration of many middle-class housewives. In 1966 she helped found the National Organization for Women (NOW), which campaigned for equal rights through the law and politics.

The more radical women's liberation movement challenged traditional roles and beauty standards — for example the protest at the Miss America contest in 1968. In Roe v Wade (1973) the Supreme Court ruled that women had a right to abortion.

evidence: 1963: The Feminine Mystique; Equal Pay Act.

sections.title: 4. Opposition to the women's movement

blocks.p: Many Americans, including many women, opposed feminism. Phyllis Schlafly led the STOP ERA campaign (from 1972) against the Equal Rights Amendment, which Congress passed in 1972. She argued it would harm traditional families and remove protections for women, such as exemption from the draft. The ERA was never ratified by enough states.
Religious and conservative groups also opposed abortion after Roe v Wade, and the 'pro-life' movement grew.

evidence: 1972: ERA passed by Congress; STOP ERA begins.

flashcards.q: Give three reasons protest movements grew in the 1960s.
flashcards.a: Baby boom and more students; civil rights example; the Vietnam draft; youth culture.

flashcards.q: What was the Berkeley Free Speech Movement?
flashcards.a: 1964 student protest against a ban on political activity on campus.

flashcards.q: How did students protest against the Vietnam War?
flashcards.a: Teach-ins, burning draft cards, marches; Kent State 1970.
Equal rights for women through the law and politics.

flashcards.q: Give two legal changes for women.
flashcards.a: Equal Pay Act 1963; Civil Rights Act 1964 banned sex discrimination at work; Roe v Wade 1973.

flashcards.q: Why did Schlafly oppose the ERA?
flashcards.a: She argued it would harm traditional families and remove protections such as exemption from the draft.
